text: Quantum mechanics is certainly imposing. But an inner voice tells me that it is not yet the real thing. The theory says a lot, but does not really bring us any closer to the secret of the 'old one'. I, at any rate, am convinced that He is not playing at dice.
context: Letter to Max Born, 4 December 1926, in Irene Born's translation. Other editions render the last clause 'He does not throw dice'. The popular form 'God does not play dice' is a compression, not Einstein's sentence.

text: The weakness of the theory is, on the one hand, that it does not bring us closer to a link-up with the wave theory, and, on the other hand, that it also leaves time and direction of elementary processes to 'chance'.
context: From 'Zur Quantentheorie der Strahlung'. Einstein introduced transition probabilities himself and immediately flagged them as a weakness.

text: It is the theory which decides what we can observe.
context: Recalled by Heisenberg some forty years later, describing a conversation in Berlin in spring 1926. Heisenberg says it later helped him toward the uncertainty relations.

text: I am convinced that you have made a decisive advance with your formulation of the quantum condition, just as I am equally convinced that the Heisenberg-Born route is off the track.
context: Letter to Schrödinger, 26 April 1926. Einstein's view of matrix mechanics softened once equivalence was shown, but his unease about completeness remained.

text: Vos calculs sont corrects, mais votre physique est abominable.
context: 'Your calculations are correct, but your physics is abominable.' Lemaître's recollection (1958) of Einstein's response to the expanding-universe paper, in conversation at this council.

text: spukhafte Fernwirkung
context: 'Spooky action at a distance' — letter to Born, 3 March 1947. Twenty years after this council; the 1927 Einstein has not said it.

text: Have you noticed that Bohm believes (as de Broglie did, by the way, 25 years ago) that he is able to interpret the quantum theory in deterministic terms? That way seems too cheap to me.
context: Letter to Born, 12 May 1952 — Einstein's reaction to Bohm's revival of de Broglie's 1927 theory.

text: If, without in any way disturbing a system, we can predict with certainty (i.e., with probability equal to unity) the value of a physical quantity, then there exists an element of physical reality corresponding to this physical quantity.
context: The EPR 'criterion of reality'. The paper was drafted by Podolsky; Einstein later said the essential point was smothered by formalism.

text: …an independent reality in the ordinary physical sense can neither be ascribed to the phenomena nor to the agencies of observation.
context: From the published Como lecture (Nature, 1928), written in English. A version of this argument was what Bohr presented at the Solvay council.

text: The very nature of the quantum theory thus forces us to regard the space-time co-ordination and the claim of causality, the union of which characterises the classical theories, as complementary but exclusive features of the description, symbolising the idealisation of observation and definition respectively.
context: Como lecture as published in Nature (1928). Bohr revised the text repeatedly; minor wording differs between versions.

text: But still, it cannot be for us to tell God how he is to run the world.
context: Heisenberg recalls Bohr answering Einstein's remarks about God and dice at this council. The popular version — 'Einstein, stop telling God what to do' — is not attested in that form. Treat as the gist of a remembered exchange.

text: Genauere Überlegung zeigt, daß die Wahrscheinlichkeit dem Quadrat der Größe Φ proportional ist.
context: Note added in proof: 'More careful consideration shows that the probability is proportional to the square of the quantity Φ.' The Born rule entered physics as a footnote.

text: The motion of particles conforms to the laws of probability, but the probability itself is propagated in accordance with the law of causality.
context: Born's formulation of how determinism survives in the new theory — at the level of the probability wave, not the particle.

text: I myself am inclined to give up determinism in the world of atoms. But that is a philosophical question for which physical arguments alone are not decisive.
context: From the preliminary collision paper. Born frames the renunciation as a choice, not a proof.

text: We regard quantum mechanics as a closed theory, whose fundamental physical and mathematical assumptions are no longer susceptible of any modification.
context: Conclusion of the joint Born–Heisenberg report, read at this council. English after Bacciagaluppi & Valentini; wording differs slightly between translations. Joint authorship: it speaks for Heisenberg too.

text: The more precisely the position is determined, the less precisely the momentum is known in this instant, and vice versa.
context: The uncertainty paper, in the Wheeler–Zurek translation.

text: I believe that the existence of the classical 'path' can be pregnantly formulated as follows: The 'path' comes into existence only when we observe it.
context: The uncertainty paper, in the Wheeler–Zurek translation.

text: …quantum mechanics establishes the final failure of causality.
context: From the closing section of the uncertainty paper, where Heisenberg argues that the premise of the causal law — exact knowledge of the present — cannot in principle be satisfied.

text: The more I think about the physical portion of Schrödinger's theory, the more repulsive I find it.
context: Letter to Pauli, 8 June 1926. The letter goes on in much blunter language about Schrödinger's claims of visualisability. A private letter between friends, not a public statement.

text: I knew of his theory, of course, but I felt discouraged, not to say repelled, by the methods of transcendental algebra, which appeared difficult to me, and by the lack of visualizability.
context: Footnote in Schrödinger's equivalence paper, referring to Heisenberg's matrix mechanics.

text: If all this damned quantum jumping were really to stay, I should be sorry I ever got involved with quantum theory.
context: Recalled by Heisenberg from Schrödinger's visit to Copenhagen in October 1926, when Bohr pressed him for days. Wording is Heisenberg's reconstruction.

text: I would not call that one but rather the characteristic trait of quantum mechanics, the one that enforces its entire departure from classical lines of thought.
context: On entanglement, in the paper that introduced the English word. Eight years after this council.

text: One can look at the world with the p-eye and one can look at it with the q-eye, but if one opens both eyes, then one goes crazy.
context: Letter to Heisenberg, 19 October 1926. Some translations end 'one goes wrong'. Written months before the uncertainty paper.

text: Well, our friend Dirac, too, has a religion, and its guiding principle is 'There is no God and Dirac is His prophet.'
context: Heisenberg places this in an evening conversation among the younger physicists at this council, after Dirac had argued against religion. A good story, recorded forty years later.

text: That he may sometimes have missed the target in his speculations, as, for example, in his hypothesis of light quanta, cannot really be held too much against him.
context: From the proposal for Einstein's election to the Prussian Academy, signed by Planck, Nernst, Rubens and Warburg. Shows how isolated the light-quantum hypothesis still was in 1913.

text: Briefly summarized, what I did can be described as simply an act of desperation.
context: Letter to R. W. Wood, 1931, looking back on December 1900. Later testimony — the 1927 Planck has not written this.

text: Like a game of chess, Einstein all the time with new examples. In a certain sense a sort of Perpetuum Mobile of the second kind to break the UNCERTAINTY RELATION. Bohr from out of philosophical smoke clouds constantly searching for the tools to crush one example after the other. Einstein like a jack-in-the-box: jumping out fresh every morning.
context: Letter to his students, five days after the council closed — the eyewitness account on which most later retellings depend.

text: I am almost without reservation pro Bohr and contra Einstein. His attitude to Bohr is now exactly like the attitude of the defenders of absolute simultaneity towards him.
context: Same letter. Ehrenfest was one of Einstein's closest friends; the judgement cost him something.

text: Einstein, I am ashamed of you; you are arguing against the new quantum theory just as your opponents argue about relativity theory.
context: Heisenberg's recollection of Ehrenfest speaking to Einstein at this council. Consistent in substance with Ehrenfest's own letter of 3 November 1927.

text: What is proved by impossibility proofs is lack of imagination.
context: From 'On the impossible pilot wave'.

text: The proof of von Neumann is not merely false but foolish!
context: Magazine interview; the substance is stated carefully in Bell's 1966 paper.

text: Was the wavefunction of the world waiting to jump for thousands of millions of years until a single-celled living creature appeared? Or did it have to wait a little longer, for some better qualified system … with a PhD?
context: From 'Against measurement' — Bell's objection to giving observation a fundamental role.

text: I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.
context: Messenger Lectures, Cornell, 1964.

text: …a phenomenon which is impossible, absolutely impossible, to explain in any classical way, and which has in it the heart of quantum mechanics. In reality, it contains the only mystery.
context: On the two-slit experiment with electrons.

text: Nature isn't classical, dammit, and if you want to make a simulation of nature, you'd better make it quantum mechanical, and by golly it's a wonderful problem, because it doesn't look so easy.
context: Closing of 'Simulating Physics with Computers', from a 1981 talk.

text: Not only does God play dice, but he sometimes confuses us by throwing them where they can't be seen.
context: From the Hawking–Penrose debate lectures. Hawking later (2004) reversed his view that black holes destroy information.
